title: Losing faith in New Atheism: ‘The God Delusion’ 20 years on
gist: Twenty years after The God Delusion, Guy Stagg argues New Atheism has faded because it was a product of the post-9/11 moment and never grasped why people believe, offering no substitute guidance. Its lasting legacy may be sharper religious thinking, and with rapid AI-driven change — exemplified by Leo XIV's widely read encyclical on AI — religious ideas may become more, not less, relevant this century.

themes.theme: The God Delusion as a post-9/11 phenomenon

insights.claim: Richard Dawkins's The God Delusion, published 20 years ago, sold over three million copies in 35 languages and led New Atheism, alongside Christopher Hitchens, Sam Harris and Daniel Dennett.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Benchmark for how an intellectual movement scaled through bestsellers, debates and YouTube.

insights.claim: New Atheism's rise was enabled by the post-9/11 moment, when wars in Afghanistan and Iraq made Islamic extremism seem the major threat to a post-Cold War order of globalisation and prosperity.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Intellectual fashions track the dominant perceived threat of their era.
insights.quote: the West was suddenly threatened by outdated religious beliefs
insights.locator: Academics have been writing sceptical books

insights.claim: Twenty years on, the terrorism threat is dwarfed by Russian and Chinese aggression, economic shocks from the GFC and pandemic, shrinking populations and an overheating planet, while Western Christianity appears in terminal decline — undermining the case that religion is an urgent threat.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Author's ranking of today's top risks: great-power conflict, demographics and climate outrank terrorism.
insights.quote: The threat from terrorism is dwarfed by the potential impact of Russian and Chinese aggression.

insights.claim: New Atheism's leaders have died or softened: Hitchens and Dennett are dead, Sam Harris launched a mindfulness meditation app, and Ayaan Hirsi Ali converted to Christianity.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Signals the movement's loss of momentum.
insights.locator: But New Atheism has also changed.

insights.claim: New Atheism was an early culture-war casualty: its free-thinking leaders clashed with followers wanting a progressive movement, and in April 2021 the American Humanist Association withdrew Dawkins's 1996 Humanist of the Year award over a tweet on gender and race identity.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Shows how identity politics fractured a previously unified secular movement.
insights.locator: New Atheism was also an early victim

insights.claim: The God Delusion's core weakness is that it attacks a cartoon version of faith from American pastors and Islamic fundamentalists while ignoring theological literature and religious scientists like Aquinas, Lemaître and Mendel.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Critiques that skip the strongest opposing arguments have little staying power.
insights.quote: Most of its attacks are aimed at the cartoon version of faith conjured by American pastors and Islamic fundamentalists.
insights.locator: The God Delusion is a compelling but limited

insights.claim: In a discussion with former Archbishop of Canterbury Rowan Williams, Dawkins could not articulate a credible reason for faith, admitting he was 'rather baffled'.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Illustrates the movement's failure to understand the appeal of religion.
insights.locator: The God Delusion is a compelling but limited

insights.claim: Because it failed to appreciate the human appetite for the symbolic and non-rational, New Atheism's aggressive doubt offered no substitute guidance or sustaining ideology and so made little lasting impact.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Movements that only negate, without offering meaning, tend not to endure.
insights.quote: New Atheism’s aggressive doubt could offer no substitute guidance, nor any sustaining ideology

insights.claim: New Atheism's most lasting consequence may be better religious writing: woolly apologetics gave way to assertive defences of faith from Iain McGilchrist, sympathetic voices like Tom Holland and informed sceptics like Alex O'Connor.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Opposition strengthened the very thing it attacked — a second-order effect.
insights.quote: the most permanent consequence of the New Atheist movement may be the improved quality of religious writing and thinking

insights.claim: Thinkers across the political spectrum are returning to religious texts to address family decline, weakened community, capitalism's excesses and environmental destruction.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Religion is re-entering policy debate as a source of frameworks on social cohesion.

insights.claim: Pope Leo XIV's recent encyclical on AI found a wide audience from trade unions to the MAGA movement, as Silicon Valley races to create consciousness, defeat death and build machines with near-divine knowledge.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Religious institutions are becoming influential voices in AI ethics and could shape the political coalition around AI regulation.

insights.claim: Contrary to the Enlightenment belief that science leads society away from faith, the dizzying pace of technological change may make religious ideas more relevant this century, as people seek a fixed point or answers to what it means to be human.
insights.speaker: Guy Stagg
insights.so_what: Rapid AI-driven change may fuel demand for meaning-making institutions — a social counter-current to tech acceleration.
insights.quote: religious ideas may become more relevant over the course of the century
